title: What To Do After a Scam - Getting Money Back, Where to Report, Identity Theft Recovery
heading: If you paid with a credit or debit card
text: Contact the company or bank that issued the card right away. Use the phone number on the back of the card or the issuer's official app or website. Tell them the charge was fraudulent and ask them to reverse it and refund you. The FTC notes that federal law gives protections against unauthorized credit card use, and debit cards have similar protections. Acting quickly matters.

title: What To Do After a Scam - Getting Money Back, Where to Report, Identity Theft Recovery
heading: If you paid by bank transfer, Zelle or a payment app
text: If you sent money from your bank account, including with Zelle, report it to your bank or credit union right away. Ask them to reverse the payment and refund you. If you used a payment app such as Venmo, Cash App or PayPal, report the fraudulent transaction to the app company immediately and ask for a reversal. In every case, the FTC's advice is to contact the company that moved the money as soon as you realize it was a scam.

title: What To Do After a Scam - Getting Money Back, Where to Report, Identity Theft Recovery
heading: If you paid by wire transfer or gift card
text: For a wire through a service such as Western Union or MoneyGram, contact the service immediately. Tell them it was a fraudulent transfer and ask for a refund. MoneyGram's number is 1-800-666-3947 and Western Union's is 1-800-325-6000. For gift cards, contact the company that issued the card using the number on the back. Explain that a scammer got the card number and PIN, ask for a refund, and keep the card and receipt.

title: What To Do After a Scam - Getting Money Back, Where to Report, Identity Theft Recovery
heading: If you paid with cryptocurrency or cash
text: Contact the crypto exchange or crypto ATM company you used. Report the fraudulent transaction and ask them to reverse it, then report it to law enforcement. The FTC warns that cryptocurrency payments do not have the legal protections that credit and debit cards have. If you mailed cash, contact the US Postal Inspection Service at 1-877-876-2455 right away and ask about stopping the package. If you used another delivery service, contact that company.

title: What To Do After a Scam - Getting Money Back, Where to Report, Identity Theft Recovery
heading: If you gave a scammer your SSN or passwords
text: If a scammer has your Social Security number, go to IdentityTheft.gov. You can report the theft and get a personal recovery plan. If the number has not been misused yet, the site's data breach steps explain how to protect it. If you gave out a username and password, change the password right away, use a strong new one, and turn on two-factor authentication. If you gave remote access to your device, update your security software, run a scan and remove any threats.

title: What To Do After a Scam - Getting Money Back, Where to Report, Identity Theft Recovery
heading: Tell the FTC about the scam
text: The FTC asks people to report scams at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. It uses these reports to bring cases against scammers, spot trends, warn consumers and track what is happening in different communities. Reporting a scam to the FTC is separate from asking your bank or payment service for a refund, so do both. Immigration-related scams can also be reported to the ICE Tip Line (1-866-347-2423) and online crime to the FBI at ic3.gov.

title: What To Do After a Scam - Getting Money Back, Where to Report, Identity Theft Recovery
heading: Warning signs of identity theft
text:
The FTC lists common signs that someone is using your identity. You may stop getting a bill, which can mean someone changed your billing address. You may see charges or new bills you do not recognize, or money taken from your bank account that you did not approve. Your credit report may show accounts you never opened. Anyone who shared passport, SSN or bank details with a scam caller should watch for these signs.
Source: https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/what-know-about-identity-theft

title: What To Do After a Scam - Getting Money Back, Where to Report, Identity Theft Recovery
heading: Reporting identity theft at IdentityTheft.gov
text:
Report identity theft to the FTC at IdentityTheft.gov, or RobodeIdentidad.gov in Spanish. You can also call 877-438-4338 and press 3 for other languages. You will get a personal recovery plan with steps to follow. The site covers more than 30 types of identity theft, including tax identity theft, where a thief uses your SSN to file a tax return and take your refund. Free credit reports are available at annualcreditreport.com.
Source: https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/what-know-about-identity-theft

title: What To Do After a Scam - Getting Money Back, Where to Report, Identity Theft Recovery
heading: Credit freeze
text:
A credit freeze stops anyone, including you, from opening new credit in your name until you lift it. It is free to place and free to lift. You must contact each of the three national credit bureaus, Equifax, Experian and TransUnion, separately. The freeze stays in place until you remove it. When you need to apply for credit, you can lift it temporarily, either at all three bureaus or only at the one a lender will check.
Source: https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/what-know-about-credit-freezes-and-fraud-alerts

title: What To Do After a Scam - Getting Money Back, Where to Report, Identity Theft Recovery
heading: Fraud alerts
text:
A fraud alert tells businesses to check your identity before opening credit in your name. It is free. To place an initial fraud alert, you contact just one of the three credit bureaus, and it must tell the other two. An initial alert lasts one year and can be renewed. Identity theft victims who have an FTC identity theft report or a police report can get an extended fraud alert, which lasts seven years.
Source: https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/what-know-about-credit-freezes-and-fraud-alerts

title: What To Do After a Scam - Getting Money Back, Where to Report, Identity Theft Recovery
heading: IRS Identity Protection PIN
text:
An IRS Identity Protection PIN (IP PIN) is a six-digit number. It stops anyone else from filing a federal tax return with your SSN or ITIN. Anyone with an SSN or ITIN who can verify their identity can get one. The fastest way is through your IRS online account. Other options are Form 15227, which has income limits, or an in-person visit to a Taxpayer Assistance Center. The IP PIN is valid for one calendar year, and a new one is issued each year.
Source: https://www.irs.gov/identity-theft-fraud-scams/get-an-identity-protection-pin

title: What To Do After a Scam - Getting Money Back, Where to Report, Identity Theft Recovery
heading: The IRS never asks for your IP PIN
text:
The IRS says it will never ask for your IP PIN. Any phone call, email or text asking for it is a scam. Share the IP PIN only with your trusted tax preparer, and use it on every federal tax return you file that year. Anyone with an SSN or ITIN whose personal details were exposed in a scam can get an IP PIN to help guard against tax identity theft.
Source: https://www.irs.gov/identity-theft-fraud-scams/get-an-identity-protection-pin

title: DHS, SEVP and ICE/HSI Guidance on Imposters Targeting F-1 Students
heading: DHS will never ask for money this way
publisher: U.S. Department of Homeland Security, Study in the States (SEVP)
text: In a February 2026 advisory, DHS warned that scammers pose as DHS officials to target foreign students. DHS includes USCIS, ICE, Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) and the Student and Exchange Visitor Program (SEVP). The advisory says DHS will never ask you to transfer money to an individual person. It also says DHS will never ask you to pay fees by phone or by email. A caller or emailer who asks for either is not acting for DHS.

title: DHS, SEVP and ICE/HSI Guidance on Imposters Targeting F-1 Students
heading: Common tactics in DHS imposter scams
publisher: U.S. Department of Homeland Security, Study in the States (SEVP)
text: According to DHS, scammers may ask for your Alien Registration Number or Form I-94. They may say there is a problem with your record in the Student and Exchange Visitor Information System (SEVIS). They may demand payment by wire transfer, gift card, prepaid debit card, credit card or cryptocurrency, or ask for bank or card details. Some promise to "fix" your immigration status for a fee. These calls may show a real government number on caller ID, threaten arrest or deportation, and push you to act right away.

title: DHS, SEVP and ICE/HSI Guidance on Imposters Targeting F-1 Students
heading: How to recognize real DHS officials
publisher: U.S. Department of Homeland Security, Study in the States (SEVP)
text: Real HSI representatives, including SEVP field representatives, carry official credentials that show their photo and title. You may ask to see these credentials. If a credential seems suspicious, contact your Designated School Official (DSO) or the SEVP Response Center at 703-603-3400. Real DHS emails come from addresses ending in ".gov". They include a full signature with the sender's name, phone number and .gov email address.

title: DHS, SEVP and ICE/HSI Guidance on Imposters Targeting F-1 Students
heading: What students should do
publisher: U.S. Department of Homeland Security, Study in the States (SEVP)
text: DHS advises students who suspect a scam not to share personal or financial information and not to send money. End the call or conversation. Contact your DSO at your school's international student office. Report the contact to the ICE Tip Line at 1-866-347-2423. DSOs are asked to contact their SEVP field representative or the SEVP Response Center and to report suspicious contacts to the ICE Tip Line.

title: DHS, SEVP and ICE/HSI Guidance on Imposters Targeting F-1 Students
heading: The DSO's role and SEVIS records
publisher: U.S. Department of Homeland Security, Study in the States (SEVP)
text:
A Designated School Official is a school employee chosen by the head of an SEVP-certified school. Federal law requires DSOs to update and maintain F and M student records in SEVIS. DSOs also advise students on work authorization, travel, address changes, program extensions and other status matters. A student who is told there is a problem with their SEVIS record should check with their DSO before taking any other step. A paid caller cannot "fix" a SEVIS record.
Source: https://studyinthestates.dhs.gov/schools/get-started/designated-school-official

title: DHS, SEVP and ICE/HSI Guidance on Imposters Targeting F-1 Students
heading: SEVP never asks for gift cards or bitcoin
publisher: U.S. Department of Homeland Security, Study in the States (SEVP)
text:
A December 2022 Study in the States alert described callers posing as SEVP Response Center staff. They told students to buy gift cards, which an "agent" would supposedly collect. SEVP stated that its officials will never ask for credit card, debit card or gift card numbers, wire transfers or bank routing numbers, or ask anyone to make bitcoin deposits. The scam calls used a 703 area code. SEVP said its real calls to students come from the Washington, DC 202 area code.
Source: https://studyinthestates.dhs.gov/2022/12/students-beware-of-phone-scammers

title: DHS, SEVP and ICE/HSI Guidance on Imposters Targeting F-1 Students
heading: Scammers spoof real SEVP phone numbers
publisher: U.S. Department of Homeland Security, Study in the States (SEVP)
text:
In December 2020, SEVP warned that scammers were spoofing the real SEVP Response Center numbers, 703-603-3400 and 800-892-4829. The callers asked students about their Form I-94 and tried to get financial information. A familiar SEVP number on caller ID does not prove a call is real. SEVP advised students not to share personal or financial details with unknown callers and to contact their DSO if unsure. It also pointed victims to the HSI tip form at ice.gov.
Source: https://studyinthestates.dhs.gov/2020/12/students-watch-out-for-scammers-using-sevp-phone-numbers

title: DHS, SEVP and ICE/HSI Guidance on Imposters Targeting F-1 Students
heading: What real SEVP Portal emails look like
publisher: U.S. Department of Homeland Security, Study in the States (SEVP)
text:
Students on post-completion OPT or STEM OPT use the SEVP Portal to report their address, phone number and employer. Portal emails come from do-not-reply.SEVP@ice.dhs.gov. They cover account creation, temporary passwords, password changes, locked accounts and email changes. Each one says not to reply because the mailbox is not monitored. For help, the emails point to the SEVP Response Center at 703-603-3400 or SEVP@ice.dhs.gov.
Source: https://studyinthestates.dhs.gov/sevis-help-hub/student-records/fm-student-employment/sevis-and-the-sevp-portal/portal-email-notices

title: DHS, SEVP and ICE/HSI Guidance on Imposters Targeting F-1 Students
heading: HSI agents do not arrest people by phone
publisher: U.S. Department of Homeland Security, Study in the States (SEVP)
text:
In October 2024, HSI in Michigan and Ohio warned about people posing as HSI special agents. The callers claimed a package containing money or drugs had been intercepted in an investigation involving the victim. HSI said its agents do not call to demand account information or payment, do not threaten jail and offer payment as an alternative, and do not try to arrest people by phone. They also do not ask for Social Security, credit card or bank account numbers over the phone.
Source: https://www.ice.gov/news/releases/hsi-michigan-and-ohio-warn-scammers-impersonating-special-agents

title: DHS, SEVP and ICE/HSI Guidance on Imposters Targeting F-1 Students
heading: Passport "problem" calls and spoofed HSI lines
publisher: U.S. Department of Homeland Security, Study in the States (SEVP)
text:
In November 2021, HSI San Antonio warned that imposters were spoofing its main office number, 210-979-4500. The callers claimed the victim's passport was involved in a crime and threatened to send police to arrest them. HSI said its special agents and local police do not call people to warn them of an upcoming arrest. They do not ask for bank or credit card information, and they do not demand money to drop an investigation or cancel a warrant.
Source: https://www.ice.gov/news/releases/hsi-san-antonio-warns-public-about-spoofing-phone-calls

title: DHS, SEVP and ICE/HSI Guidance on Imposters Targeting F-1 Students
heading: How to reach the ICE Tip Line
publisher: U.S. Department of Homeland Security, Study in the States (SEVP)
text:
The ICE Tip Line is open 24 hours a day, 7 days a week at 866-DHS-2-ICE (866-347-2423) from the US and Canada. From other countries, call (802) 872-6199. Tips can also be sent through the online form at ice.gov/webform/ice-tip-form. Staff speak several languages and have access to interpreters. HSI also runs its own tip line at 877-4-HSI-TIP (1-877-447-4847) for reporting people who pose as special agents.
Source: https://www.ice.gov/tipline

title: FBI IC3 Alerts on Impersonation of Officials, Students and Deepfakes
heading: FBI warning: imposters targeting foreign students (May 2025)
publisher: Federal Bureau of Investigation, Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3)
text: In alert I-051325-PSA, dated May 13, 2025, the FBI warned about criminals targeting foreign students who are in the United States on valid F-1 visas. The scammers falsely claim the student has broken visa rules or has another immigration problem. They then threaten prosecution or deportation to get money. The alert specifically named students from the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Jordan as targets.

title: FBI IC3 Alerts on Impersonation of Officials, Students and Deepfakes
heading: Who the student-visa scammers pretend to be
publisher: Federal Bureau of Investigation, Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3)
text: According to the FBI, these scammers pose as agents of DHS, Homeland Security Investigations or USCIS. In some versions they claim to be officials of foreign governments such as the UAE or Qatar, or diplomats from the UAE Embassy in Washington, DC. They may also pose as US universities. The FBI says they spoof the phone numbers of government agencies, foreign embassies or universities. They may speak professionally and use the accent or language of the place they claim to represent.

title: FBI IC3 Alerts on Impersonation of Officials, Students and Deepfakes
heading: What the student-visa scammers ask for
publisher: Federal Bureau of Investigation, Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3)
text: Victims are told to send money to an unknown person or bank account. The scammers say the money is for processing immigration paperwork, paying university registration fees or covering legal fees. The FBI advises hanging up and calling the agency back on an official number. Be wary of look-alike web addresses such as "gov.org" that copy real .gov domains. Never share two-factor authentication codes, and do not download files from unverified sources.

title: FBI IC3 Alerts on Impersonation of Officials, Students and Deepfakes
heading: If you sent money to a student-visa scammer
publisher: Federal Bureau of Investigation, Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3)
text: The FBI asks victims to file a complaint at www.ic3.gov with as much detail as possible. If you made a bank transfer, contact your bank right away. Ask the bank to try to recall the transfer and to notify the FBI's Financial Fraud Kill Chain. When filing, include details such as the phone numbers, email addresses, account numbers, messages and payment receipts connected to the scam. The FBI's advice is to contact the bank immediately rather than wait.

title: FBI IC3 Alerts on Impersonation of Officials, Students and Deepfakes
heading: AI voice messages impersonating senior US officials
publisher: Federal Bureau of Investigation, Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3)
text:
In alert I-051525-PSA, dated May 15, 2025, the FBI said that since April 2025 criminals had been impersonating senior US officials. They used text messages ("smishing") and AI-generated voice messages ("vishing") to build trust. Then they asked targets to click links or move to another messaging platform. The FBI noted that AI voice cloning can sound almost identical to a real person. Callers should be verified independently, not trusted by voice alone.
Source: https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2025/PSA250515

title: FBI IC3 Alerts on Impersonation of Officials, Students and Deepfakes
heading: Protecting yourself from voice and text impersonation
publisher: Federal Bureau of Investigation, Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3)
text:
The FBI recommends looking up the official contact details of anyone who claims to be an official and calling them back yourself. Check email addresses, phone numbers, URLs and spelling for small changes. Look for flaws in images and videos, such as distorted hands or unnatural faces. Do not send money or cryptocurrency to someone you have only met online or by phone. Turn on multi-factor authentication, never share one-time codes, and consider a secret phrase with family.
Source: https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2025/PSA250515

title: FBI IC3 Alerts on Impersonation of Officials, Students and Deepfakes
heading: Fake FBI agents and fake IC3 sites (July 2026)
publisher: Federal Bureau of Investigation, Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3)
text:
On July 20, 2026, the FBI issued alert I-072026-PSA about criminals posing as FBI staff and as IC3 itself. They target people who were already scammed. In one version, a fake "FBI agent" contacts victims on Facebook Messenger or Telegram and sends a link to "update" an IC3 complaint. The link steals information or money. In another version, deepfake videos of senior FBI leaders send viewers to a fake copy of the ic3.gov site that collects contact and loss details.
Source: https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2026/PSA260720

title: FBI IC3 Alerts on Impersonation of Officials, Students and Deepfakes
heading: What the FBI and IC3 will not do
publisher: Federal Bureau of Investigation, Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3)
text:
The July 2026 alert says the FBI and IC3 do not reach out to victims through social media, Telegram or other messaging apps. They do not charge fees or ask for payment to recover lost money. They do not investigate crimes or return funds through social platforms. To file a real complaint, type www.ic3.gov straight into the browser instead of clicking search results or sponsored ads, and check that the address ends in .gov.
Source: https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2026/PSA260720

title: FBI IC3 Alerts on Impersonation of Officials, Students and Deepfakes
heading: Signs of a deepfake video or call
publisher: Federal Bureau of Investigation, Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3)
text:
The FBI lists several signs that a video or call may be AI-generated. Look for distorted hands, feet or faces, wrong shadows, odd watermarks and unnatural movement. On calls, listen for lag or a strange speaking rhythm. Voice cloning can sound almost exactly like someone you know. Small changes in names, URLs or email addresses are another clue. Deepfake scams often try to make you feel strong fear or urgency so you act before you check.
Source: https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2026/PSA260720

title: FTC Guidance on Government Imposter Scams
heading: How government imposter scams start
text: Government imposter scams usually begin with a call, email, text or social media message from someone who says they work for an agency. Examples include the FTC, the Social Security Administration, the IRS or Medicare. To seem real, scammers may give a fake "employee ID number" and may already know your name or address. They then say something bad will happen unless you pay or share personal information, or that you will miss out on a benefit.

title: FTC Guidance on Government Imposter Scams
heading: Payment methods only scammers demand
text: The FTC explains that government imposters insist on payment methods that are hard to trace and hard to reverse. These include wire transfers, gift cards, cryptocurrency, payment apps and cash. Scammers choose these methods because once the money is sent it is very difficult to get back. A demand to pay a government "fine" or "fee" in any of these ways is a clear sign of a scam.

title: FTC Guidance on Government Imposter Scams
heading: What real government agencies will not do
text: The FTC lists things real agencies will not do. They will not call, email, text or message you on social media to demand money or personal information. They will not threaten you with arrest or legal action to make you pay. They will not demand payment by wire transfer or gift card. They will not ask for your Social Security, bank account or credit card numbers in an unexpected contact, or suspend benefits or licenses over the phone.

title: FTC Guidance on Government Imposter Scams
heading: Caller ID can be faked
text: Your caller ID may show a government agency's real name or phone number, such as "Social Security Administration". The FTC warns that caller ID can be faked. The person calling could be anyone, anywhere in the world. A familiar number on the screen is not proof that a call is real. If a call or message might be genuine, hang up and call the agency yourself using a number from its official website.

title: FTC Guidance on Government Imposter Scams
heading: What to do when contacted
text: The FTC advises people to hang up or ignore suspicious contacts. Do not give financial or personal information to someone who contacts you out of the blue. Do not click links in unexpected messages; delete them instead. To check whether there is a real problem, contact the agency directly using a number you know is correct. If a robocall asks you to press a number to speak to someone, do not press anything.

title: FTC Guidance on Government Imposter Scams
heading: Where to report government impersonation
text: Report government imposter scams to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. You can also report them to your state attorney general, whose contact details are listed through naag.org. Reports help the FTC and its law enforcement partners find and stop scammers. If you shared personal information such as your Social Security number, go to IdentityTheft.gov. It gives step-by-step recovery and protection advice based on what was exposed, so you can act before the information is misused.

title: FTC Guidance on Government Imposter Scams
heading: "Move your money to keep it safe" is a scam
text:
A January 2024 FTC alert describes scammers who pose as bank fraud staff, the FTC, Amazon or government agencies. They claim there is suspicious activity on your account or that someone is using your identity. Then they urge you to move money to a "safe" account, into cryptocurrency or into gold to protect it. Real financial institutions will never ask you to move money to protect it. Check any warning by calling the number on your card or statement.
Source: https://consumer.ftc.gov/consumer-alerts/2024/01/did-someone-tell-you-move-or-transfer-your-money-it-could-be-scam

title: FTC Guidance on Government Imposter Scams
heading: Fake agents sending photo IDs and badges
text:
In June 2026, the FTC warned about scammers who pose as FTC employees and promise to recover money lost in earlier scams. To gain trust, they text photos of fake employee ID cards and badges. The FTC says its real employees do not contact people by text or messaging apps like WhatsApp. They do not send photos of their IDs, and they do not charge money to recover scam losses. A badge photo sent over chat is not proof of identity.
Source: https://consumer.ftc.gov/consumer-alerts/2026/06/real-ftc-employee-wont-text-you-their-photo-id-verify-their-identity

title: FTC Guidance on Government Imposter Scams
heading: Scale of imposter scams in 2025
text:
The FTC reported in June 2026 that people said they lost $3.5 billion to imposter scams in 2025. Reported losses to government impersonators were about $920 million, up from $789 million in 2024. Overall fraud losses reported to the FTC were about $16 billion, up about 25% from 2024. Scammers reached people by text, phone, email, social media and search results. The FTC repeated that it will never demand money, make threats, tell you to transfer money, or promise a prize.
Source: https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2026/06/ftc-data-show-people-reported-losing-3-point-5-billion-imposter-scams-2025

title: FTC Guidance on Government Imposter Scams
heading: Government imposter reports keep rising
text:
A May 2026 FTC alert said the agency received more than one million imposter scam reports in 2025. It was the ninth year in a row that imposter scams were the most reported fraud. Reports of government imposter scams went up about 40%. Many of these were fake toll-payment texts that threatened late fees or registration suspension. The FTC advises contacting the real agency using contact details you look up yourself, not details from the message.
Source: https://consumer.ftc.gov/consumer-alerts/2026/05/new-trends-reports-imposter-scams

title: FTC Guidance on Job Scams, Task Scams and Fake Check Scams
heading: Never pay to get a job
text: The FTC's main rule for job seekers is simple: do not pay for the promise of a job. Honest employers, including the federal government, will never ask you to pay to get a job. Fees for "training", "certification", "starter kits", equipment or guaranteed placement are signs of a scam. The FTC also notes that honest placement firms do not usually charge job candidates. Information about federal and Postal Service jobs is free to everyone.

title: FTC Guidance on Job Scams, Task Scams and Fake Check Scams
heading: Common job scam formats
text: The FTC describes several common job scams. Work-from-home offers promise thousands of dollars a month for little effort, then sell useless kits or training. Reshipping jobs, often called "quality control" or "virtual assistant" roles, have you receive packages bought with stolen cards and send them on, sometimes overseas, which makes you part of a fraud. Other scams include fake mystery shopper jobs, reselling luxury goods, and fake nanny, caregiver or assistant postings.

title: FTC Guidance on Job Scams, Task Scams and Fake Check Scams
heading: How to check a job offer
text: Before accepting a job, the FTC suggests searching the company name with words like "scam", "review" or "complaint". Talk the offer over with someone you trust. Refuse any request to pay up front. Never deposit a check from an employer and then send part of the money somewhere else. Good places to look for jobs include USAJobs.gov, CareerOneStop and USA.gov. Report job scams to ReportFraud.ftc.gov or to your state attorney general.

title: FTC Guidance on Job Scams, Task Scams and Fake Check Scams
heading: What a task scam is
text:
Task scams, also called gamified job scams, start with an unexpected text, WhatsApp, Telegram or social media message. It offers easy online "work" such as "optimization" or "product boosting". You complete tasks in an app or website and see a "commission" for each click. The scammer may pay a small amount, often $5 to $20, so the job seems real. The growing earnings shown in the app are fake.
Source: https://consumer.ftc.gov/consumer-alerts/2025/08/how-spot-and-avoid-task-scams

title: FTC Guidance on Job Scams, Task Scams and Fake Check Scams
heading: The task scam trap: deposit to unlock earnings
text:
At some point the scammer says you must deposit your own money, usually in cryptocurrency, to unlock the next set of tasks or withdraw your earnings. Even after you deposit, the money cannot be withdrawn, and your real money is gone. The FTC advises ignoring unexpected job messages on text, WhatsApp or Telegram, because real employers will not recruit that way. Never pay to get paid. No honest company pays people just to like or rate things online.
Source: https://consumer.ftc.gov/consumer-alerts/2025/08/how-spot-and-avoid-task-scams

title: FTC Guidance on Job Scams, Task Scams and Fake Check Scams
heading: Job offer texts in 2026
text:
An April 2026 FTC alert described fake recruiters who text people claiming to work for well-known companies. They offer remote jobs such as "online assessor" or a vague "remote position". They often state a daily or weekly pay rate but give no real details about the work. Instead of sending a link, they ask you to reply "YES" or "INTERESTED". Later they ask for money, through either a fake check you must partly pay back or tasks that require a deposit.
Source: https://consumer.ftc.gov/consumer-alerts/2026/04/job-offer-text-probably-scam

title: FTC Guidance on Job Scams, Task Scams and Fake Check Scams
heading: Fake recruiters impersonating real employers
text:
A July 2025 FTC alert warned that scammers pose as recruiters for major employers. They send fake interview invitations and offer letters by email or text. Real recruiters usually write from a corporate email address, not a personal Gmail or Yahoo account. Scammers often ask for your driver's license, Social Security number or bank details before any real interview, sometimes calling it "employment paperwork". Real employers interview you before asking for direct-deposit information.
Source: https://consumer.ftc.gov/consumer-alerts/2025/07/job-scammers-are-looking-hire-you

title: FTC Guidance on Job Scams, Task Scams and Fake Check Scams
heading: How fake check scams work
text:
In a fake check scam, someone sends you a check, often for more than you are owed. They ask you to deposit it and send part of the money back or on to someone else. The reason might be job supplies, prize "taxes" or an "overpayment". Banks must make deposited funds available quickly. But the FTC warns that seeing the money in your account does not mean the check is good. A fake check can take weeks to bounce, and you must repay the bank.
Source: https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/how-spot-avoid-and-report-fake-check-scams

title: FTC Guidance on Job Scams, Task Scams and Fake Check Scams
heading: Fake check variants aimed at job seekers
text:
The FTC lists common fake check stories. In mystery shopping scams, you deposit a check and wire money to "retailers". In personal assistant scams, you buy gift cards and send the PINs to your "employer". In car wrap advertising scams, you pay a supposed decal installer. Other versions involve prize fees and marketplace overpayments. Never use money from a deposited check to buy gift cards or crypto, or to send a wire. If you already sent money, contact the payment service right away and report it at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
Source: https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/how-spot-avoid-and-report-fake-check-scams

title: Rental Listing, Scholarship and Tuition Payment Scams
heading: How rental listing scams work
text: The FTC describes two main rental scams. In one, scammers copy a real listing's photos, description or virtual tour and put their own contact details on it. In the other, they post an ad for a place that does not exist or is not for rent. They may take application fees, deposits or rent. They may also collect Social Security and driver's license numbers for identity theft, or push victims to sign up for paid credit monitoring.

title: Rental Listing, Scholarship and Tuition Payment Scams
heading: Rental scam red flags
text: Warning signs include rent far below the going rate, pressure to decide quickly, and a "landlord" who cannot meet or show the property, often because they say they are out of the country. Others are demands for payment by wire transfer, gift card or cryptocurrency, and requests for personal information before any lease is agreed. A listing for a home that is actually for sale, not for rent, is another warning sign the FTC mentions.

title: Rental Listing, Scholarship and Tuition Payment Scams
heading: Protecting yourself when renting
text: Search the address online together with the owner's or company's name. If the same place is listed under different names, that is a warning sign. Search the owner's name with "scam", "complaint" or "review". Visit the property, or ask someone you trust to visit it, before signing or paying. Get the contract before sending a deposit. Do not give your SSN or credit details until the rental terms are agreed. Report rental scams to local police, the listing website, ReportFraud.ftc.gov and your state attorney general.

title: Rental Listing, Scholarship and Tuition Payment Scams
heading: Scholarship scam warning signs
text:
The FTC says scholarship scams often begin with a social media post, email or letter saying you have been "selected" for a scholarship or aid package. Some invite you to a high-pressure seminar. Never pay to apply for a scholarship. Typical scam lines include claims that the scholarship is guaranteed or your money back, that you only need to give a card or bank number to "hold" it, or that you are a "finalist" in a contest you never entered.
Source: https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/how-avoid-scholarship-and-financial-aid-scams

title: Rental Listing, Scholarship and Tuition Payment Scams
heading: Financial aid "processing fee" scams
text:
Some companies charge fees to get students grants, loans or work-study, which are free to apply for. Some even fill in the FAFSA with false information, which can expose the student to penalties of up to $20,000 or prison. The FTC advises completing the FAFSA yourself, never sharing your FSA ID, and asking your school's financial aid office before paying anyone. Scholarship and aid scams can be reported at ReportFraud.ftc.gov and to your state attorney general.
Source: https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/how-avoid-scholarship-and-financial-aid-scams

title: Rental Listing, Scholarship and Tuition Payment Scams
heading: Tuition payment scams aimed at international students
text:
Flywire, an international tuition payment company, warns about scams aimed at international students. Some scammers offer discounted tuition payments or offer to pay tuition for the student. Others pose as government agents and threaten visa problems unless a payment is made right away. Some approach students on campus, in visa lines or at admitted-student events. Others make documents with fake co-branded logos claiming a link to a university. Fake job offers may also recruit students as "money mules" who move funds for criminals.
Source: https://www.flywire.com/resources/six-steps

title: Rental Listing, Scholarship and Tuition Payment Scams
heading: Paying tuition safely
text:
Flywire's advice is to pay only through secure (https) sites and providers your school has confirmed. Do not share login details with payment processors you have not verified. Check who is asking before giving sensitive information. Be skeptical of offers that seem too good to be true, such as discounted tuition. Report suspected fraud to both your university and the police. The main message is to check any payment processor directly with your school before using it.
Source: https://www.flywire.com/resources/six-steps

title: SEVP and ICE on Fraudulent OPT and STEM OPT Employers
heading: SEVP broadcast on STEM OPT employer fraud (March 2026)
publisher: Student and Exchange Visitor Program (SEVP), U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement
text: On March 23, 2026, SEVP sent Broadcast Message 2603-02, "STEM OPT Employer Fraud", to all SEVIS users. It asks DSOs to watch for fraud by STEM OPT employers, especially IT recruitment firms, consulting firms and staffing agencies. SEVP said it is working with DHS partners to investigate fraud among these businesses. It repeated a point from the 2016 STEM OPT rule: these kinds of employment arrangements are a fraud concern and are generally not a good fit for STEM OPT.

title: SEVP and ICE on Fraudulent OPT and STEM OPT Employers
heading: What investigators found at suspect employers
publisher: Student and Exchange Visitor Program (SEVP), U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement
text: During recent site visits, SEVP and HSI found many signs of fraud at suspect STEM OPT employers. Business locations were empty and unused. Some employers listed private homes as worksites, but no employees were there. Human resources and payroll staff were "offshore". Company officials knew little about the business, or made inconsistent and contradictory statements about it and about the students. Many students said they were hired on STEM OPT but never actually showed up for work. Phone numbers did not work.

title: SEVP and ICE on Fraudulent OPT and STEM OPT Employers
heading: Red flags of a fraudulent OPT employer
publisher: Student and Exchange Visitor Program (SEVP), U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement
text: SEVP lists red flags for possibly fraudulent employers. The company website is vague, with no examples of client work, contact details or social media. The job duties do not match what the employer told the school. The work location does not look suitable or does not match the address on Form I-983. A little-known employer hires a large group of F or M students from one school. The work is done remotely or through apps such as WeChat.

title: SEVP and ICE on Fraudulent OPT and STEM OPT Employers
heading: Consequences and how to report employer fraud
publisher: Student and Exchange Visitor Program (SEVP), U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement
text: SEVP warns that employers and students involved in suspected fraud risk being referred for administrative or criminal investigation by HSI and the Department of Justice. DSOs are asked to remind students to contact them with questions about a recruiter's advice. Students or DSOs who think an employer is not following the rules can report it to the ICE Tip Line, the SEVP Response Center (703-603-3400 or 1-800-892-4829, SEVP@ice.dhs.gov) or a local Project Campus Sentinel agent.

title: SEVP and ICE on Fraudulent OPT and STEM OPT Employers
heading: Reporting wage and working-condition problems
publisher: Student and Exchange Visitor Program (SEVP), U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement
text: SEVP's March 2026 message also tells students they can report concerns about wages or working conditions directly to the US Department of Labor. That is separate from reporting suspected immigration fraud to ICE or SEVP. So a student who is not paid as promised, or whose working conditions seem wrong, has an official federal agency to contact. The SRC is open Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. Eastern, except federal holidays.

title: SEVP and ICE on Fraudulent OPT and STEM OPT Employers
heading: ICE site visits in Northern Virginia (October 2025)
publisher: Student and Exchange Visitor Program (SEVP), U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement
text:
In October 2025, ICE announced site visits to employers of F-1 students in Northern Virginia. HSI reported evidence of employer fraud. It found worksites that did not function or were staged, and supervisors who did not know the rules for employing foreign students. One employer said it ran dozens of OPT positions from a home in the Virginia suburbs. ICE said it would step up investigations to reduce fraud and security risks in the OPT program.
Source: https://www.ice.gov/news/releases/ice-conducts-visits-employers-northern-virginia-ensure-legal-compliance-when-hiring

title: SEVP and ICE on Fraudulent OPT and STEM OPT Employers
heading: Paying for fake proof of employment is visa fraud
publisher: Student and Exchange Visitor Program (SEVP), U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement
text:
In July 2019, ICE announced the indictment of a businesswoman who set up two companies, Findream LLC and Sinocontech LLC. The companies did not provide any services and did not employ the people who answered their ads. For a fee, they gave customers written proof of employment so the customers could stay in the US on student and work visas. At least 2,685 customers listed these companies as their employer, and the companies received at least $2 million. Each visa fraud count carries up to 10 years in prison.
Source: https://www.ice.gov/news/releases/chinese-businesswoman-indicted-student-visa-work-visa-fraud-charges

title: SEVP and ICE on Fraudulent OPT and STEM OPT Employers
heading: How fake-employer schemes recruited students
publisher: Student and Exchange Visitor Program (SEVP), U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement
text:
According to ICE, the 2019 scheme advertised on a China-based job website and in a WeChat group aimed at job hunters in North America. The customers were F-1 students seeking to extend their employment authorization, and people seeking H-1B work visas. In this scheme the job seeker paid the "employer" for paperwork, which is the reverse of real employment. Prosecutors charged the scheme as conspiracy to commit visa fraud and visa fraud.
Source: https://www.ice.gov/news/releases/chinese-businesswoman-indicted-student-visa-work-visa-fraud-charges

title: SEVP and ICE on Fraudulent OPT and STEM OPT Employers
heading: Students arrested for claiming nonexistent employers
publisher: Student and Exchange Visitor Program (SEVP), U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement
text:
In October 2020, ICE announced Operation OPTical Illusion. Fifteen nonimmigrant students were arrested for fraudulently using the OPT program. They claimed to work for companies that do not exist. Arrests took place in several states and the Washington, DC area. ICE said it would continue checking whether students who got jobs through OPT were complying with their immigration status. Listing a fake or paid-for employer puts the student, not just the company, at legal risk.
Source: https://www.ice.gov/news/releases/ice-arrests-15-nonimmigrant-students-opt-related-fraud

title: OPT and STEM OPT Rules (USCIS and SEVP)
heading: OPT basics for F-1 students
text:
Optional Practical Training (OPT) lets F-1 students work in jobs related to their studies. Students can get up to 12 months of OPT at each education level. Any pre-completion OPT used reduces the post-completion time left. To apply, the student's DSO must first enter an OPT recommendation in SEVIS. The student then files Form I-765, Application for Employment Authorization, with USCIS. All OPT work must be directly related to the student's major field of study.
Source: https://www.uscis.gov/working-in-the-united-states/students-and-exchange-visitors/optional-practical-training-opt-for-f-1-students

title: OPT and STEM OPT Rules (USCIS and SEVP)
heading: OPT filing window and start of work
text:
A student may file for post-completion OPT up to 90 days before finishing the program. The filing must be no later than 60 days after completing the degree, and only after the DSO has entered the recommendation in SEVIS. A student may not start pre- or post-completion OPT work until USCIS approves Form I-765 and the student has the Employment Authorization Document (EAD). Post-completion OPT may be part time, at least 20 hours a week, or full time.
Source: https://www.uscis.gov/working-in-the-united-states/students-and-exchange-visitors/optional-practical-training-opt-for-f-1-students

title: OPT and STEM OPT Rules (USCIS and SEVP)
heading: STEM OPT extension length and filing
text: Students with a qualifying STEM degree can apply for a 24-month extension of post-completion OPT. USCIS says to file up to 90 days before the current OPT authorization ends, and within 60 days after the DSO enters the STEM OPT recommendation in SEVIS. If the extension is filed on time and the current OPT ends while it is pending, work authorization is automatically extended for 180 days.

title: OPT and STEM OPT Rules (USCIS and SEVP)
heading: Unemployment day limits
text: During the first period of post-completion OPT, a student may have up to 90 days of unemployment. The STEM OPT extension adds 60 more days, so the limit is 150 days across post-completion OPT and STEM OPT combined. SEVP's STEM OPT guidance gives the same numbers: 90 days during the first post-completion OPT period plus 60 extra days during the 24-month extension. Students track their employment and report it through their DSO or the SEVP Portal.

title: OPT and STEM OPT Rules (USCIS and SEVP)
heading: STEM OPT employer requirements
text: A STEM OPT employer must be enrolled in E-Verify, the USCIS online system for confirming employment eligibility. The employer must also have a valid Employer Identification Number (EIN). It must complete Form I-983, Training Plan for STEM OPT Students, with the student, and have a real (bona fide) employer-employee relationship with the student. It must pay the student at a level comparable to similarly situated US workers.

title: OPT and STEM OPT Rules (USCIS and SEVP)
heading: No "employer in name only" or volunteer STEM OPT
text:
USCIS says a STEM OPT employer may not be the student's employer in name only. The student also may not work for the employer as a "volunteer". The SEVP STEM OPT overview adds that STEM OPT students must work at least 20 hours a week for each employer. The employer must provide formal training and learning objectives. An offer of unpaid STEM OPT, or of a letter that lists a company as employer without real work, does not meet these rules.
Source: https://studyinthestates.dhs.gov/stem-opt-hub/additional-resources/stem-opt-extension-overview

title: OPT and STEM OPT Rules (USCIS and SEVP)
heading: Students cannot sign their own Form I-983
text:
SEVP has reminded students that the STEM OPT employer must give all the employer signatures on Form I-983. A STEM OPT student cannot sign the employer attestation on their own behalf. Start-up businesses can take part, but only if they meet all the regulatory requirements and are enrolled in E-Verify. Be suspicious of any "employer" who asks the student to fill in or sign the employer section.
Source: https://studyinthestates.dhs.gov/2016/09/reminder-stem-opt-students-must-train-bona-fide-employers

title: OPT and STEM OPT Rules (USCIS and SEVP)
heading: STEM OPT reporting duties
text:
STEM OPT students must check in with their DSO every six months to confirm that their SEVIS information is correct. This includes legal name, address, employer name and address, and employment status. Email reminders are sent 30 days before each check-in is due. Changes, including losing a job, must be reported to the DSO within 10 days. Students must also complete self-evaluations at 12 and 24 months, signed by both student and employer.
Source: https://studyinthestates.dhs.gov/stem-opt-hub/for-students/students-stem-opt-reporting-requirements

title: OPT and STEM OPT Rules (USCIS and SEVP)
heading: Changing employers on STEM OPT
text:
When a STEM OPT student starts a new job, they must submit a new Form I-983 to the DSO within 10 days of starting. The new employer must also be enrolled in E-Verify. A final evaluation for the previous employer is due within 10 days after that job ends. Students must also report big changes to the training plan, such as a new employer EIN, a pay cut not linked to hours, or a large cut in hours.
Source: https://studyinthestates.dhs.gov/stem-opt-hub/for-students/students-stem-opt-reporting-requirements

title: OPT and STEM OPT Rules (USCIS and SEVP)
heading: The SEVP Portal for OPT reporting
text:
The SEVP Portal lets students on post-completion OPT and STEM OPT meet their reporting duties. Through it they can update their address, phone number and employer details. After OPT is approved in SEVIS, the portal emails the student a link to create an account. Students can still edit their contact and employment details for up to 15 days after their OPT end date. DSOs help with the process but do not create portal accounts themselves.
Source: https://studyinthestates.dhs.gov/sevis-help-hub/student-records/fm-student-employment/sevis-and-the-sevp-portal

title: OPT and STEM OPT Rules (USCIS and SEVP)
heading: Checking whether an employer uses E-Verify
text:
Anyone can look up employers enrolled in E-Verify with the E-Verify Employer Search tool on e-verify.gov. Results show the employer's legal name, any "doing business as" name, whether the account is enrolled or terminated, enrollment dates, workforce size and hiring site states. The data is reported by employers themselves. A search by trade name may fail if the company enrolled under its legal name, and not every location of a company may take part.
Source: https://www.e-verify.gov/e-verify-employer-search

title: University International Student Office Scam Alerts, 2024-2026 (summary)
heading: CU Boulder, June 2026: fake USCIS "AR-11" calls and emails
publisher: Various university international student offices (summarized; not official government guidance)
text:
In June 2026, CU Boulder's ISSS described an ongoing scam about Form AR-11, the change-of-address form. Callers whose caller ID shows USCIS say the student never filed an AR-11 and threaten immediate deportation. They ask for photos of immigration documents, contact details, bank information and Social Security numbers, and use pressure to keep victims on the line. Follow-up emails use a gov-looking display name but come from a Gmail address. ISSS stresses that real officials will not stop you from contacting your school.
Source: https://www.colorado.edu/isss/2026/06/01/scam-alert-uscis-ar-11-phone-call-and-email

title: University International Student Office Scam Alerts, 2024-2026 (summary)
heading: CU Boulder, June 2026: spoofed ICE and police calls
publisher: Various university international student offices (summarized; not official government guidance)
text:
A second June 2026 CU Boulder alert describes a two-step scam. First, a caller spoofing a New York ICE office number claims there is an arrest warrant because of an error in the student's I-94 record and threatens removal. Then a call spoofing the Boulder Police non-emergency line warns of a warrant and a visit to the student's home. Callers may give fake names and "ICE badge numbers" and ask for documents and bank details. ISSS advises hanging up and reporting the call.
Source: https://www.colorado.edu/isss/2026/06/01/scam-alert-spoofed-calls-ice-and-boulder-police-department

title: University International Student Office Scam Alerts, 2024-2026 (summary)
heading: CU Boulder, October 2024: "unpaid university fee" calls
publisher: Various university international student offices (summarized; not official government guidance)
text:
CU Boulder warned in October 2024 about calls spoofed to look like they came from the university. The callers told international students they owed an unpaid CU Boulder fee and would be deported immediately if they did not pay. They first asked for passport and visa details, then told students to send money through Zelle. ISSS said any threatening call like this claiming to be from CU Boulder is fraudulent. It asked students to report such calls to ISSS and to the HSI tip line.
Source: https://www.colorado.edu/isss/2024/10/18/scam-alert-unpaid-cu-boulder-fees-phone-scam

title: University International Student Office Scam Alerts, 2024-2026 (summary)
heading: Genuine SEVP unemployment warnings can also sound urgent
publisher: Various university international student offices (summarized; not official government guidance)
text:
Not every urgent message is a scam. In May 2025, CU Boulder ISSS explained that SEVP may email OPT students who are near or over the unemployment limit. These real messages can say that SEVP will mark the SEVIS record "terminated" if it is not updated within 15 days. They do not ask for payment. ISSS advised students to check the email linked to their SEVP Portal account, report employment promptly, and contact ISSS if they are unsure whether a message is real.
Source: https://www.colorado.edu/isss/2025/05/27/optional-practical-training-opt-and-unemployment

title: University International Student Office Scam Alerts, 2024-2026 (summary)
heading: Wayne State, April 2025: fake CBP and ICE calls with gift cards
publisher: Various university international student offices (summarized; not official government guidance)
text:
In April 2025, Wayne State University's Office of International Programs described a student who got a call from someone claiming to be from Customs and Border Protection. The caller said the student had not reported a change of address and threatened prison and deportation. A second caller posed as ICE and also threatened to freeze the student's bank accounts. The student was told to buy gift cards, and the scammers kept asking for more. The office lists secrecy demands and "your SEVIS is terminated" claims as red flags.
Source: https://oip.wayne.edu/news/scam-emails-and-calls-target-international-students-and-scholars-66119

title: University International Student Office Scam Alerts, 2024-2026 (summary)
heading: SJSU: a catalog of scam scripts
publisher: Various university international student offices (summarized; not official government guidance)
text:
San Jose State's ISSS keeps a list of scams reported by students. They include callers posing as the Social Security Administration, saying a student's SSN was used in crimes, and USCIS imposters who ask about the AR-11 along with SSN digits, passport and bank details. Others are DHS callers with spoofed caller ID who demand a fine in Apple or eBay gift cards, "911" callers who want Google Play cards, and calls claiming to be from the Chinese consulate. A fake USCIS email came from a non-government ".link"-style address.
Source: https://sjsu.edu/isss/resources/scam-alerts.php

title: University International Student Office Scam Alerts, 2024-2026 (summary)
heading: SJSU: academic-integrity and job scams
publisher: Various university international student offices (summarized; not official government guidance)
text:
SJSU also flagged scams that are not government imposters. One online message claimed the student had an academic integrity violation, demanded payment and threatened expulsion. SJSU noted that real conduct notices come only through its official student conduct system. Another scam used Google Chat to pose as HR staff at real companies. They offered jobs with no interview or background check and then sent a check to buy "home office equipment", a fake check pattern.
Source: https://sjsu.edu/isss/resources/scam-alerts.php

title: University International Student Office Scam Alerts, 2024-2026 (summary)
heading: Drexel, February 2026: relaying the DHS advisory
publisher: Various university international student offices (summarized; not official government guidance)
text:
In February 2026, Drexel's international student office passed on the DHS advisory about scammers posing as DHS officials. It listed the usual tactics: asking for A-numbers or I-94s, claiming SEVIS problems, demanding wire, gift card, prepaid card, credit card or crypto payments, and offering to fix status for a fee. Drexel told students not to share information or send money, to end the contact, tell their DSO, report to the ICE Tip Line, and contact campus public safety.
Source: https://drexel.edu/studentlife/student-success/international-student-support/announcements/2026/February/DHS-Advisory-Scams

title: University International Student Office Scam Alerts, 2024-2026 (summary)
heading: University of Washington, December 2024: fake academic integrity office
publisher: Various university international student offices (summarized; not official government guidance)
text:
In December 2024, UW's International Student Services warned about emails from a made-up "UW Academic Integrity Department". The emails accused students of academic violations and suggested their visa status was at risk. The scammers copied the ISS newsletter header to look official. UW advised students not to respond or share personal information, to check the sender through official UW channels, and to report suspicious messages to ISS or the UW Police Department.
Source: https://iss.washington.edu/alert-new-scam-targets-international-students/

title: University International Student Office Scam Alerts, 2024-2026 (summary)
heading: Common threads across university alerts
publisher: Various university international student offices (summarized; not official government guidance)
text: Across these 2024-2026 alerts, the same patterns repeat. Spoofed caller ID shows real agency, police or university numbers. Scammers make claims about AR-11, I-94, SEVIS or unpaid fees, and threaten arrest, deportation or frozen accounts. They demand gift cards, Zelle, wire transfers or crypto, ask for passport, SSN and bank details, and tell victims to stay on the line or keep quiet. Every office gives the same advice: hang up, do not pay, and contact your international student office directly.

title: USCIS Avoid Scams, Official Channels and Reporting
heading: What USCIS will never do
text: USCIS says it will not ask anyone to transfer money to an individual person. Fees are not paid outside the official USCIS process, such as through your USCIS online account. USCIS forms are free to download from the official website. A person who offers to sell you a USCIS form, or asks you to pay a private person to "process" a USCIS filing, is not acting for USCIS.

title: USCIS Avoid Scams, Official Channels and Reporting
heading: You do not need a paid middleman
text: USCIS points out that you do not need a representative to file forms. People can file forms and represent themselves. If you want help, only licensed attorneys or accredited representatives of organizations recognized by the Department of Justice may represent you. USCIS advises checking a representative against the official lists before hiring them. Offers to speed up a case for a fee, or promises of quick benefits, are red flags.

title: USCIS Avoid Scams, Official Channels and Reporting
heading: Trust only .gov websites
text: USCIS tells people to trust only official .gov websites and communications. Scammers often build sites on .com, .org, .net or .info addresses that look like government pages. Emails with spelling mistakes, unexpected attachments, or offers to expedite a case for money are common signs of a scam. Scammers also try to make the immigration process seem more complicated than it is so that victims will pay for "help".

title: USCIS Avoid Scams, Official Channels and Reporting
heading: Official USCIS email sender
text:
On June 18, 2024, USCIS changed its email update service. Messages now come from uscis@messages.dhs.gov. The old sender domain, public.govdelivery.com, is no longer used. USCIS said the change was made to strengthen security and help people confirm that messages are real. An email claiming to be a USCIS update that comes from a free webmail account or a non-government domain is suspicious.
Source: https://www.uscis.gov/i-9-central/form-i-9-related-news/uscis-updates-have-a-new-email-address

title: USCIS Avoid Scams, Official Channels and Reporting
heading: What real USCIS case notifications contain
text:
When someone files Form G-1145, USCIS can send an email or text saying it has accepted an application. These e-Notifications include the receipt number and explain how to get case status information. They do not include personal information, not even the person's name, because email and text are not secure. A real notification will not ask you to reply with personal data, pay a fee, or call a private phone number.
Source: https://www.uscis.gov/g-1145

title: USCIS Avoid Scams, Official Channels and Reporting
heading: Checking a case status yourself
text:
You can check a case status yourself with USCIS Case Status Online, reached through uscis.gov. A USCIS receipt number has 13 characters: three letters, such as EAC, WAC, LIN, SRC, NBC, MSC or IOE, followed by 10 numbers. A free USCIS online account at my.uscis.gov shows recent case actions. The USCIS Contact Center number is 1-800-375-5283. Checking status this way is safer than trusting a link or phone number in a message.
Source: https://www.uscis.gov/tools/checking-your-case-status-online

title: USCIS Avoid Scams, Official Channels and Reporting
heading: Spoofed calls impersonating USCIS
text:
USCIS warns that scammers use technology to make their caller ID look like a government agency or another trusted number. These callers may ask about your immigration status or case and try to get personal or financial information. Real USCIS staff will not pressure you to act immediately or threaten you with consequences. If you are unsure, hang up and contact USCIS through its official channels.
Source: https://www.uscis.gov/save/current-user-agencies/news-alerts/fraud-alert-reports-of-scam-calls-impersonating-uscis

title: USCIS Avoid Scams, Official Channels and Reporting
heading: Where to report immigration scams
text:
USCIS suggests several places to report. Report to your state consumer protection office or attorney general, and to the Federal Trade Commission at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. If you lost money or property, also report to local police. Fake websites or social media accounts that claim to be part of USCIS can be reported by email to uscis.webmaster@uscis.dhs.gov. Many states also let people report scams anonymously.
Source: https://www.uscis.gov/scams-fraud-and-misconduct/avoid-scams/report-immigration-scams

title: USCIS Avoid Scams, Official Channels and Reporting
heading: Reporting will not hurt your case
text: USCIS states that reporting a scam will not affect your immigration application or petition. This matters for international students, who may fear that contacting authorities will put their status at risk. Phishing emails pretending to be USCIS can be forwarded to USCIS.Webmaster@uscis.dhs.gov. Fraud by people posing as immigration legal providers can also be reported to the Executive Office for Immigration Review fraud program.

title: USCIS Common Scams
heading: Government impersonators
text: Scammers pretend to be USCIS officials to frighten immigrants and visa holders into paying money or handing over personal information. USCIS states that it contacts people only through official government channels. It does not reach out through a person's private social media accounts. A message that claims to be from USCIS but arrives through a personal Instagram, Facebook, WhatsApp or similar account should therefore be treated as a scam until it is confirmed through an official USCIS channel.

title: USCIS Common Scams
heading: How USCIS accepts payments
text: USCIS takes online payments only through a person's official USCIS online account and through Pay.gov. It will never ask anyone to send money to an individual person. USCIS does not accept Western Union, MoneyGram, PayPal, Venmo or gift cards. USCIS also says it will not ask for payment over the phone or by email. Any caller or emailer who wants an immigration fee, fine or penalty paid through one of these methods is not USCIS.

title: USCIS Common Scams
heading: Official email addresses and websites
text: Email addresses belonging to the US government always end in ".gov". USCIS warns that scammers set up fake USCIS social media pages, fake emails and fake websites that copy the agency's look. A sender address or link that ends in something other than .gov, such as a free webmail account or a .com or .org site using the USCIS name, is a warning sign. USCIS runs official social media accounts on X (Twitter), Instagram, YouTube, Facebook and LinkedIn.

title: USCIS Common Scams
heading: Student scams
text: USCIS lists scams aimed at foreign students. These include fake universities and threatening phone calls made to international students. Callers may claim there is a problem with a student's immigration record and push for quick payment or personal details. Students who get an unexpected call like this should not pay or share information. They should check with their school's international student office or with USCIS through official channels.

title: USCIS Common Scams
heading: Job offer scams
text: Fake employers may offer jobs, often overseas, and ask for money up front before the "job" starts. USCIS lists this among its common scams. The "employer" may promise that the job will lead to a visa, work permit or other immigration benefit. A job offer that requires the applicant to pay first, especially one tied to an immigration benefit, is a strong sign of fraud. Real employers do not sell jobs to applicants.

title: USCIS Common Scams
heading: Form I-9 email scams
text: USCIS warns of phishing emails that pretend to come from USCIS and ask employers for employment eligibility verification (Form I-9) information. These messages use USCIS branding to look real. A student starting an OPT job may see similar requests passed on by an employer. Employers and employees should confirm any such request through official USCIS channels before replying or sending documents. Suspicious USCIS-branded emails can be forwarded to USCIS.Webmaster@uscis.dhs.gov.

title: USCIS Common Scams
heading: "Jumping the line" and expediting schemes
text: Some businesses falsely claim they have special connections at USCIS. They say they can speed up a case or skip the normal processing line if the applicant pays a fee. USCIS lists this as a scam. Students waiting on an OPT or STEM OPT decision may be tempted by such offers, but the claim of a private "inside contact" who can move a case faster for money is itself a warning sign. Case status can be checked for free through official USCIS tools.

title: USCIS Common Scams
heading: Notarios publicos fraud
text: In many Latin American countries, a "notario publico" is a lawyer. In the United States, notaries public are not authorized to give legal services. USCIS warns that unlicensed notaries and consultants sometimes falsely claim they can give immigration legal advice or file cases. Only licensed attorneys or accredited representatives may give immigration legal help. Before paying anyone for immigration help, check that they are a licensed attorney or an accredited representative.

title: USCIS Common Scams
heading: Visa lottery and other program scams
text: The State Department runs the diversity visa lottery and will never email someone to say they were selected. USCIS also says it does not routinely send emails announcing diversity visa approvals. Scammers also target humanitarian programs by charging fees that do not exist. For example, USCIS does not charge a fee to file Form I-134A, and scammers have demanded fees before TPS re-registration notices were even published.

title: USCIS Common Scams
heading: Where to report a USCIS-related scam
text: USCIS recommends reporting suspected immigration scams to the Federal Trade Commission. Suspicious emails that pretend to be from USCIS can be forwarded to USCIS.Webmaster@uscis.dhs.gov. Victims of coerced labor or human trafficking can call the National Human Trafficking Hotline at 888-373-7888. USCIS also lists its official social media accounts, so a student can check whether a page or profile using the USCIS name is genuine before trusting a message sent from it.
